title: HackerRank Profile and Assessments Multiple Choice
description: Problem-Solving Score, certifications, badges, rank, IPK, OA pacing, and edge-case handling from module 06.

questions.prompt: A profile's Problem-Solving Score grows to 82. What does that number tell you about the same profile's SQL score?

options.text: SQL score must also be high, since HackerRank scores are shared across domains
Nothing — each domain (Problem Solving, SQL, JavaScript, ...) accumulates its own score separately
SQL score is automatically set to zero once another domain passes 80
The two scores are always within 10 points of each other

questions.explanation: Score accumulates per domain, not as one global number — a strong Problem Solving score says nothing about SQL or any other domain.

questions.prompt: A candidate fails a Skill Certification attempt on their first try, then passes on the second attempt. What shows on the public profile?

options.text: Two badges — one for each attempt
No badge, because the first attempt failed
One badge, from the passed attempt only
A partial-credit badge reflecting the average of both attempts

questions.explanation: Certifications are pass/fail as a whole. Only a passed attempt produces a visible certificate badge; a failed attempt simply doesn't add one.

questions.prompt: A skill badge shows progress `19/20` for its current tier. What is true about this badge right now?

options.text: It is `complete`, since 19 is close enough to 20
It is `in-progress`, because `earned` (19) has not reached `total` (20) yet
It has `failed`, like a certification attempt would
It resets to `0/20` because it is so close to completion

questions.explanation: A badge tier is `complete` only when `earned` equals `total`. Any value strictly less than `total`, even `19/20`, is still `in-progress` — there is no failure state for badges.

questions.prompt: Two profiles show global ranks `100` and `101`. Using the tiers `rank <= 100 -> top-100`, `rank <= 1000 -> top-1000`, else `open`, which tiers do they land in?

options.text: Both `top-100`, since 100 and 101 are nearly identical
Rank `100` is `top-100`; rank `101` is `top-1000`
Both `top-1000`, because the boundary is exclusive
Rank `100` is `top-1000`; rank `101` is `open`

questions.explanation: The `top-100` boundary is inclusive at `100`, so rank `100` still qualifies; rank `101` falls just past it into `top-1000`.

questions.prompt: You know you are weak on array manipulation but strong on strings. What is the most efficient way to use the Interview Preparation Kit (IPK)?

options.text: Work through the kit strictly top-to-bottom regardless of topic
Only solve `Warmup` problems, since they build momentum for everything else
Route directly into the `Arrays` topic track to target the known weak spot
Skip IPK entirely and rely on random practice challenges instead

questions.explanation: IPK is organized topic-first specifically so you can route into the track that targets a known gap, instead of grinding topics you're already strong in.

questions.prompt: You are 16 minutes from the end of a 90-minute Online Assessment (OA) with two unstarted questions. Using thresholds `< 15 min -> rush`, `< 45 min -> pace`, `>= 45 min -> plan`, what mode applies, and what does it suggest?

options.text: `plan` mode — there's still plenty of time to read every question fully first
`pace` mode — keep moving steadily rather than starting a risky new approach
`rush` mode — abandon the current question immediately
The mode does not matter since OAs allow pausing the timer

questions.explanation: 16 minutes is still `>= 15`, so it's `pace`, not `rush`. That suggests staying steady rather than gambling on a fresh approach this late, while OAs are typically single-window and non-pausable.

questions.prompt: An Implementation-tagged problem states five separate rules. A candidate's solution passes the general case but loses points on hidden tests. What is the most likely cause, based on why Implementation problems lose points?

options.text: The candidate picked an algorithm with the wrong time complexity
The candidate missed one of the spec's explicit rules, not the overall algorithm idea
Implementation problems cannot be scored with hidden test cases
The language runtime silently changed the expected output format

questions.explanation: Most points lost on Implementation problems come from missing a rule the spec explicitly lists, not from choosing the wrong algorithm — a checklist mindset catches this before submitting.

questions.prompt: Before submitting a solution, which four edge-case categories should a quick pre-submission checklist cover?

options.text: Fast, slow, cached, uncached
Empty, zero, negative, single-element input
First run, second run, retry, timeout
Uppercase, lowercase, mixed case, empty string only

questions.explanation: HackerRank grades per test case, and hidden cases usually probe empty input, a zero value, a negative value, or a single-element input where general-case logic quietly breaks.
